# SpotifyArchiver

Used as a University Project. Involves experimenting with different Ai CLI practices for software development. The outcome of which will produce a console application with the functionality of archiving Spotify Playlists to local json files.

***This report presents the results of a major internal project at Zircon Software Ltd to evaluate targeted AI‑assisted command‑line interface (CLI) practices in controlled trials, with the aim of identifying those that deliver measurable gains in productivity and architectural compliance for embedded and remote software development workflows.***

***Using Gemini CLI as the test platform, five practices: Persistent Context File, Prompt Scaffolding, Code Explanation & Variant Generation, Assertion‑First Prompting, and Layer Scoped Sub Tasking were selected based on literature and industry case studies and trialled against two control baselines across a theoretical minimum viable product. Performance was assessed through quantitative metrics and qualitative acceptance surveys.***

***Results show that certain structured, scope restricting AI CLI practices significantly reduce delivery time while maintaining strict adherence to Clean Architecture and CQRS principles. Layer Scoped Sub Tasking and Assertion First Prompting proved the most impactful, leading to organisational changes such as the adoption of standard multi layered project structures, checklist\-based AI CLI integration, and formalised context maintenance. Practices with lower gains remain under consideration for further trials in more complex scenarios.***

***The project confirms the hypothesis that controlled evaluation of specific AI‑CLI practices can identify that worthy of adoption as standard organisational methods, providing Zircon with a repeatable framework for assessing emerging approaches, safeguarding maintainability, and strengthening its competitiveness in a rapidly evolving industry.***

# 1\. Foundation {#1.-foundation}

## 1.1. Introduction {#1.1.-introduction}

Zircon Software Ltd operates within a constantly changing and highly competitive technological environment, delivering embedded systems for sectors including transportation, defence and industrial control. The company’s reputation with long‑standing clients is built on consistent delivery, deep technical expertise and exceptionally high-quality standards. However, the rate at which technology is changing has increased drastically in recent years, with tools and methods driven by artificial intelligence (AI) becoming readily available to our competitors. Many are adopting new software development practices that allow faster delivery without sacrificing quality, influencing client expectations for responsiveness, flexibility, and cost efficiency. Without proactive investment in productivity, Zircon risks seeing its current advantages dissipate in the market.

Innovation has always been an important pillar for Zircon, helping to create a great reputation within the industry. However, recent industry reports show that the wider software sector is evolving rapidly in its use of development tooling, with many organisations adopting AI‑assisted tools to enhance productivity. These tools vary significantly in their level of integration, with some just being online web portals such as ChatGPT with use being down to the individuals preference, and others being embedded into formal workflows such as the AI enhanced Integrated Development Environment (IDE) Cursor.

Zircon’s current adoption pattern mirrors this mixed approach with pockets of early experimentation, but no ormalized strategy yet in place. From this experimentation, lightweight command‑line interface (CLI) tools have emerged as a particularly strong match for Zircon’s operating environment. Zircon’s projects vary significantly, with some taking place in remote, resource‑constrained build workflows where heavier integrated development environments are not always practical or possible. CLI‑based AI tools are easy to deploy in a variety of environments and integrate seamlessly into these processes, offering the ability to generate code, draft documentation, propose designs and in some cases directly test programs, all with minimal disruption to established workflows.

| Capability / Practice | Industry Trend | Zircon Current State | Relative Position |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| General AI use (e.g., ChatGPT web UI) | Widely available, mixed adoption patterns | Informal, individual-driven use | On par |
| AI-assisted CLI tooling | Increasing targeted adoption in niche workflows | Limited pilots using Gemini CLI | Slight lag |
| Standardised AI workflows | Adopted by some, but not universal | None at present | Behind some peers |
| Prompt engineering knowledge sharing | Emerging in a minority of organisations | Ad-hoc, undocumented | On par |
| Secure deployment practices | Varies, sometimes relaxed for speed | Strong, established controls | Ahead in some areas |

*Figure 1\. Gap Analysis \- Industry Trends vs Zircon's Current State*

This insight into the wider industry aligns with Zircon’s own experiences. Informal experimentation with tools such as Gemini CLI and ChatGPT Codex has already demonstrated clear potential, rapidly producing boilerplate code, offering design assistance within areas Zircon has limited experience with, supplying instant documentation drafts and helping implement test scenarios. The potential benefits are vast, but the lack of structured practices across the organisation has caused inconsistent results, varied quality, and difficulty in accurately measuring productivity improvement. In this state, wider adoption would risk embedding inefficient habits into the organisation.

This study is designed to establish and validate a standardised set of best practices for AI CLI use specific to Zircon’s needs. To ensure familiarity the emerging tool, Gemini CLI, already present within Zircon will be used across all experiments. An internal usage survey showed that, of the developers using any AI CLI tooling, four regularly used Gemini CLI, one used ChatGPT Codex, and twenty‑two did not use AI CLI tools at all. Each practice will be trialled and evaluated to ensure productivity gains are measurable, repeatable, and aligned with our standards. This will be achieved using the SMART framework:

| Type | Condition |
| :---- | :---- |
| Specific | Identify, design and document best practices for effective use of AI CLI Tools in code generation, and testing workflows. |
| Measurable | Evaluate outcomes using quantitative metrics (completion time, error count, and architecture compliance scores) and qualitative metrics (Technology Acceptance Model scores). |
| Achievable | Run rapid cycle trials against a single, self‑contained internal project with a clearly defined backlog of tickets representing a theoretical minimum viable product (MVP). Comparing results to a set of controls. |
| Relevant | Supports Zircon’s strategic objective to remain at the forefront of innovation, enhancing productivity without compromising quality. |
| Time-based | Structure implementation cycles so that each deliverable is completed within one to two working days, enabling swift evaluation, actionable learning, and integration into broader workflows without loss of momentum. |

*Figure 2\. SMART Framework*

This experimental approach has been selected for fast and focused learning allowing findings to be utilised immediately within the organisation. By concentrating trials on a single small internal project, scope and complexity are fully controlled while ensuring findings are directly caused by the differences in practice. A predetermined ticket set will represent a complete theoretical MVP that is realistic to Zircon’s work based projects and provide clear benchmarks for delivery speed, defect rates and workflow efficiency. Each ticket within the backlog represents a feature and will be used to test a different practice, enabling direct comparison and rapid identification of the methods that deliver the most improvements.

Although the work is entirely internal and not client‑facing, the same standards of ethical and professional conduct that underpin all Zircon projects will be ensured. The purpose of adopting AI‑assisted practices in this context is not to reduce headcount or seek efficiency through job cuts whilst maintaining output, but rather to improve productivity and output in order to maintain Zircon’s competitive position within a quickly evolving market. AI‑generated outputs will go through the same peer review and automated validation checks as manually written work. All artefacts will be stored within secure repositories to preserve integrity and traceability. Documentation will record precisely where AI assistance was applied and how many turns it took to produce a useable result. This transparent approach ensures that the results are both credible and reproducible, forming a reliable foundation for future adoption.

By implementing structured best practices into a controlled experimentation phase, Zircon aims to gain a framework for AI CLI integration and the knowledge needed to guide business strategy. The ability to measure, refine and scale the most effective methods will enable faster delivery, safeguard quality, and strengthen Zircon’s position as an innovative, trusted technology partner in a rapidly evolving market.

This all boils done to the hypothesis that evaluating targeted AI‑CLI practices in controlled trials will identify those that deliver measurable gains in productivity and architectural compliance, providing a foundation for their adoption as standard methods in Zircon’s workflows.

## 1.2. Literature Review {#1.2.-literature-review}

Conducting a literature review provides a structured means of aggregating credible evidence on a subject, enabling practises to be founded on tested knowledge rather than assumption. Where emerging technologies are being trialled, the process mitigates the risk of incorrectly trialling technologies or practices by identifying proven techniques, known limitations, and environmental constraints prior to implementation.

This review examines theoretical and technical sources on AI CLIs and the technology they are built on, including large language models (LLMs), as well as their integration into software development workflows, with outcomes directly informing practices for Zircon’s internal experimentation. By aggregating findings across LLM theory, tooling implementation strategies, and existing software development methodological adaptations, the review highlights practices that enhance productivity and code quality whilst reducing incorrect use of the tool.

To support structured analysis, findings are examined through three categories:

* Fundamental LLM Concepts \- technical principles and constraints imposed by the LLMs that drive AI enhanced CLIs.  
* Research-derived Practices \- strategies evidenced in academic and industry trials.  
* Methodology-embedded Practices \- integrations of LLM tooling into established business processes.

*The following sections of the literature review uses the terms AI CLIs and LLMs interchangeably, as AI CLI capabilities are determined by the underlying LLM technologies that drive them.*

### 1.2.1. Fundamental LLM Concepts {#1.2.1.-fundamental-llm-concepts}

The core capability of any AI CLI tool is determined by the LLM that powers its natural language processing (NLP) engine. A token is the name given to the smallest unit of text the model processes, typically a word fragment or short sequence of characters, and all inputs and outputs are handles as sequences of these tokens. LLMs provide comprehension, reasoning, and generation ability, enabling a CLI tool to interpret prompts and produce relevant outputs.

#### *1.2.1.1. Transformer architecture and token prediction*

The transformer architecture introduced by Vaswani et al. (2023) enables parallel processing of tokens in a prompt. It uses attention mechanisms to assign greater weight to tokens that are more relevant than others in the same input sequence, allowing the model to relate and prioritise information across the entire prompt. This is particularly important when natural language and source code appear together, as in many CLI‑driven tasks. However, this computed attention is lost once the model receives a new prompt, the weighting and associations from previous inputs are not retained. As a result, any context from earlier exchanges must be re‑included or summarised to ensure it is considered during subsequent processing.

#### *1.2.1.2. Context window limitations*

An LLM’s outputs are bounded by its maximum context window, the number of tokens it can attend to at once, meaning excess prompt content is truncated (Dao et al., 2022). For iterative CLI workflows, this requires chunking or summarising inputs to avoid loss of critical project information such as dependencies or test results.

#### *1.2.1.3. Prompt engineering*

Reynolds & McDonell (2021) found that prompts with explicit roles, constraints, and detailed context yield more accurate outputs. Without an IDE’s built in environment context, CLI prompts must fully encapsulate instructions, style requirements, and acceptance criteria to reduce rework.

### 1.2.2. Strategies & Practices from Research and Case Studies {#1.2.2.-strategies-&-practices-from-research-and-case-studies}

Case studies and academic trials offer directly transferable strategies for CLI based AI workflows:

#### *1.2.2.1. Context persistence*

Ziegler et al. (2022) found, LLMs can “forget” earlier steps unless context is reinstated in subsequent prompts. Embedding prior specifications, code fragments, or outputs into follow up requests maintains accuracy across multi turn interactions.

#### *1.2.2.2. Prompt scaffolding*

White et al. (2023) found that breaking complex tasks into a chain of smaller prompts increased accuracy and reduced defects. In CLI workflows, layered prompting allows the model to focus on individual objectives before integrating results.

#### *1.2.2.3. Code explanation comparison*

Savelka et al. (2023) found that having models explain their generated code and produce alternatives improves correctness and developer confidence. In CLI practice, each generation could include self-explanation and variants for review.

#### *1.2.2.4. Assertion first prompting*

Dakhel et al. (2023) found producing unit tests before code improves alignment with requirements. For CLI workflows, requesting runnable tests first constrains subsequent code to satisfy defined correctness criteria.

### 1.2.3. Adaptation to Development Methodologies {#1.2.3.-adaptation-to-development-methodologies}

Integrating AI CLI tools into established methodologies requires preserving core software development principles while augmenting execution with AI CLI capabilities.

#### *1.2.3.1. Test Driven Development*

Dakhel et al. (2023) found LLM generated unit tests show that AI tools can contribute to TDD by providing test scaffolds ahead of implementation. By embedding this capability into CLI prompts, teams can sustain TDD without increasing cycle time, using automatically generated tests to validate both AI produced and developer written code against agreed specifications.

#### *1.2.3.2. Abstraction enforcement*

Esposito et al. (2025) found that, due to a lack of architecture specific training datasets, LLM-generated artefacts risk breaching established abstraction boundaries, leading to unwanted coupling between layers causing maintainability and scalability to be more difficult. With methodologies typically used by Zircon such as Clean Architecture and heavy use of layered designs, these issues can affect quality and compromise long term productivity. For CLI workflows, enforcing abstraction means making layer scope explicit in prompts.

Across the reviewed categories, the literature points to several consistent requirements for successful AI CLI integration. This includes active management of context, task decomposition, explicit verification loops, and adherence to architectural principles such as abstraction enforcement. For Zircon, embedding these practices into the MVP trial will provide a fair evaluation of how AI CLI tools affect productivity, code quality, and developer workflows.

## 1.3. Methodology {#1.3.-methodology}

Establishing a methodology is important because it provides a clear, repeatable structure for testing practices under realistic conditions. This design directly supports Objective 2 of the SMART goals outlined earlier, establishing repeatable AI CLI standards, while ensuring results remain relevant to Zircon’s workflow.

The methodology follows the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle to ensure iterative development and improvement of CLI‑based practices. The Plan phase, informed by the competitive gap analysis within the introduction, identifies AI tooling as a strategic area for productivity enhancement. The Do phase applies selected practices based on the literature review in controlled runs. The Check phase measures outcomes against defined control metrics, and the Act phase implements any relevant learnings within the organisation whilst planning improvements for the potential next iteration of experimentation.

### 1.3.1. Experimental Project Selection {#1.3.1.-experimental-project-selection}

To model a practical but manageable scenario, the baseline for all tests will be a small three‑layer Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) application:

* Presentation Layer — interface and delivery mechanisms.  
* Application Layer — orchestration and business logic.  
* Data Access Layer — persistence and integration with data sources.

These layers follow Clean Architecture principles where dependencies must flow inward from outer layers towards the core domain, ensuring upper layers rely on abstractions rather than concrete implementations. This preserves separation of concerns and maintainability. 

The project size is constrained so that each feature can be fully developed within 1-2 days, supporting objective 3 of the SMART goals. This keeps experiments short without oversimplifying, and allows several complete runs to occur in quick succession.

Each ticket within the theoretical MVP encapsulates its own completion criteria providing a definition of “done”. The ensures that the stopping point for every feature is known, allowing delivery speed and compliance to be measured at a specific endpoint.

### 1.3.2. Evaluation Framework and Metrics {#1.3.2.-evaluation-framework-and-metrics}

All implementations will be logged in a standardised evaluation table to ensure consistency, objective comparisons, and traceability across runs, directly supporting the SMART goal of measurability and reproducibility.

| Practice ID | Practice | Branch Name | Contextual Link | Completion Time | Error Count | CLEAN Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Outcome Summary | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

*Figure 3\. Evaluation Table Structure*

#### *1.3.2.1. Completion Time*

Measured, to a resolution of a minute, from the start of implementation to successful compile and run with a complete set of passing tests. This provides a consistent productivity comparison across practices.

#### *1.3.2.2. Error Count*

Total number of compile-time and runtime errors encountered during implementation, used to assess whether AI involvement reduces or increases fault incidence.

#### *1.3.2.3. Clean Architecture Compliance*

Determined through static analysis enforcing Clean Architecture rules and the Staircase pattern:

* Dependencies must only go inwards (Presentation to Application to Data layer).  
* No upward references are allowed (Application to Presentation Layer).  
* Upper layers must depend on only the abstractions of lower layers.  
* Third Party Dependencies used by the implementation should not be depended on by the abstraction

#### *1.3.2.4. CQRS Compliance*

CQRS compliance will be assessed manually during review sessions rather than through automated static analysis. This approach is taken because the checks are semantic based and dependent on the developer’s intent, meaning automated checks will likely produce high rates of false positives without any validation specific to the feature.

The manual review will verify that:

* Commands contain no read operations, i.e. no querying of repositories  
* Queries contain no write operations, i.e. no usage of insert or update commands on repositories  
* Asymmetric layering will be used with all operations using the shortest layer traversal available to ensure the program is performant.

#### The result will be logged with a classification of Pass or Fail together with any relevant notes in the outcome summary.

#### *1.3.2.5. Outcome Summary*

Concise notes capturing observations such as ease of implementation, issues encountered, or notable AI suggestions.

#### *1.3.2.6. Classification*

#### A run classifies as Pass if:

* Clean Architecture review returns a static analysis result of equal to or greater than 85%.  
* Manual CQRS Review results in a Pass.  
* The error count at compile time and runtime is less than or equal to 2 non-blocking issues.

Any run failing one or more of these conditions will be classified as Fail. This ensures architectural compliance is maintained whilst the number of errors introduced during implementation is manageable and non-blocking.

####  *1.3.2.7. Qualitative Feedback \- TAM Survey*

After each run, a short Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) survey will be completed immediately after PR review sessions of the completed implementations. The survey will include:

* Perceived Usefulness (1-5) — extent the practice helped achieve the goal.  
* Perceived Ease of Use (1-5) — how straightforward the practice felt.  
* Optional Comments — notes on any friction points, unexpected benefits, or contextual factors influencing their rating.

Integrating this user centred feedback alongside quantitative scores allows an assessment of whether a technically beneficial practice is likely to be readily adopted by developers.

### 1.3.3. Potential Flaws and Mitigation Strategies {#1.3.3.-potential-flaws-and-mitigation-strategies}

While the design aims to minimise uncontrolled variation, certain factors could still influence outcomes if not addressed. These are outlined below, alongside practical measures that aim to keep the results meaningful.

#### *1.3.3.1. Learning Effect*

Implementing the same feature three times is likely to make the developer naturally faster in later implementations.

Mitigation: Timing begins only from the first line of coding to a successful compile-and-run. Planning and design phases are excluded, and the same environment, toolchain, and dataset are used for all runs. This keeps measured time closer to core implementation effort rather than accumulated familiarity.

#### *1.3.3.2. Single‑Developer Bias*

Relying on one developer limits generalisability and may reflect individual strengths or blind spots.

Mitigation: This study purposefully uses a single developer to reduce variability during initial trials. Results will be balanced against findings from a broader TAM survey across multiple team members run during scheduled pull request (PR) review sessions, providing a wider view on adoption viability.

#### *1.3.3.3. Tool Familiarity Effect*

Extended use of a new AI CLI during the experiment could improve its apparent performance over time.

Mitigation: Each practice is completed in its entirety before the next begins, and control implementations are performed first. This keeps learning from the experimental runs from leaking into the controls, and reduces cross‑contamination between workflows

The methodology ensures that each experiment runs under consistent, realistic conditions. The three‑layer CQRS baseline is familiar enough to be relevant but complex enough to reveal compliance issues. 

Metrics and compliance scoring are captured in a single framework, both scores matter to Zircon’s long‑term project health. The TAM survey adds the human perspective, recognising that developer acceptance is as important as productivity in deciding whether a practice should be adopted across the organisation.

# 2\. Execution {#2.-execution}

## 2.1. Design & Implementation {#2.1.-design-&-implementation}

### 2.1.1. Overview of Project {#2.1.1.-overview-of-project}

The experimental project to be developed is a three-layer, Clean, CQRS console application named Spotify Archiver. The presentation layer provides a terminal interface for all user interaction, the application layer handles interactions with the Spotify API, and the data access layer handles data persistence using a local database.

CQRS was selected for its separation of concerns and suitability for iterative change, it provides a means of complexity within a small project due to supporting asymmetric layering, the practice of having layers independent of the layer above them. This means that layers can be skipped when required which in some cases makes the program more performant. This helps to make the experiments realistic to the kind of projects worked on at Zircon, where small details make a big difference. Additionally, the staircase pattern is implemented by separating layers into assemblies that encapsulate the layer’s abstraction and implementation ensuring that the layer above is only dependent on the abstraction of the layer below.

An example of asymmetric layering and the staircase pattern can be seen when observing the operational and dependency flows within the Architecture Diagram. Here, the query skips the Application layer, whilst the command passes through it demonstrating the asymmetric nature. This layer skipping can be done with both commands and queries depending on the context of the operation. The programs interface driven design and layer boundaries will enable the controlled application of individual practices and realism of a project typical of Zircon.

![][image1]

*Figure 4\. Architecture Diagram (with Dependency & CQRS Flows)*

Before the experiment began, the full solution structure was scaffolded to support reproducibility and provide an initial separation of layers:

![][image2]

*Figure 5\. Solution Structure*

By separating the solution into the distinct Presentation, Application, and Data Access layers we can provide a means of enforcing Clean architecture. Whilst these are good software development practices, they will also make it easier to catch when unnecessary and unwanted dependencies occur during experiments.

### 2.1.2. Practices to be Tested {#2.1.2.-practices-to-be-tested}

This section outlines the AI CLI practices derived from the literature review that will be trialled within the development cycles. Each practice is associated with a single feature of the Spotify Archiver application, allowing any observed differences from the control branches to be attributed to that practice alone.

#### *2.1.2.1. Persistent Context File*

Ziegler et al. (2022) and Dao et al. (2022) highlight a reoccurring limitation in LLM‑driven development, the model’s lack of persistent detail from earlier exchanges, especially once context exceeds the token window. In interactive CLI workflows, this comes as repeated loss of key project information such as architecture decisions, data contracts, coding standards, and dependencies. Establishing a context file within the repository acts as a persistent, high‑value memory store. By aggregating such context into a single file and appending it into new prompts, important context will be re-run through the alerting mechanisms of the model providing a means of maintaining conventions across multi‑turn sessions.

This practice will be demonstrated on the Spotify Authentication Flow feature. This feature enables the Archiver to securely connect to a Spotify account, request authorisation, and store short‑term access tokens for subsequent playlist requests. This feature relies on third party dependencies increasing the scope of context the tool will have to maintain, making it a fitting test. 

Figure 6 shows the memory content of the AI CLI tool, this will be injected into every prompt sent to the tool.

![][image3]

*Figure 6\. AI CLI Persistent Context*

#### *2.1.2.2. Prompt Scaffolding*

White et al. (2023) found that breaking complex tasks into sequenced smaller prompts that encapsulate small tasks significantly reduces error rates and improves code accuracy. In high‑complexity scenarios, models are overloaded when required to produce complete solutions in one shot. Prompt scaffolding mitigates this by addressing the work one task at a time, with the output of one stage informing the next. This allows for more targeted instructions and reduces logical conflicts between stages.

This practice will be tested on the Query Playlist feature, a feature involving the presentation layer and application layer. This feature will also involve setting up the entry point to the application, as well as the command line interactions that will allow the user to interact with the system. This makes it a great example of a feature that could benefit from prompt scaffolding by breaking the feature down into smaller components as shown in Figure 7

![][image4]

*Figure 7\. Query Playlists Feature Decomposition*

#### *2.1.2.3. Code Explanation and Variant Generation*

Savelka et al. (2023) found that explaining generated code and offering alternative implementations improves both code correctness and developer confidence. Requesting explanations in the prompts allows the developer to detect logical or architectural inconsistencies earlier. Requesting for variants provides design alternatives without manual rewrite, widening the solution space while maintaining efficiency.

This practice will be tested with the Fetch Archived Playlists feature, a feature that utilises the presentation and data access layer to query archived playlists present in the local database. This should implement asymmetric layering to traverse from the presentation layer directly to the data access layer. This is an important performance consideration that could be missed; by having the tool explain the code generated it could help the tool consider such aspects during implementation.

![][image5]

*Figure 8\. Code Explanation and Variant Generation Prompt*

Figure 8 shows the initial prompt for this practice, using git-style markers to demonstrate different variations allows developers to review both and quickly dictate which they prefer in a familiar manor.

#### *2.1.2.4. Assertion‑First Prompting*

Dakhel et al. (2023) found that generating unit tests before implementation enforces TDD. By first producing runnable, criteria driven tests, the CLI is required to create code that passes these explicit behavioural checks. This should ensure that all requirements are met and architecture is up held during development.

This practice will be used for the List Songs from Archived Playlist feature. This feature is a good test as the tool should again be using asymmetric layering, skipping over the application layer during implementation. By Writing tests first, the tool should have a clear idea of what components in the solution are required to implement the feature and what is unnecessary such as the application layer for this example.

![][image6]

*Figure 9\. Assertion First Prompt*

Figure 9 shows the initial prompt for this practice, specifying that the tool should first write any relevant modifications to the abstractions before writing the tests. This ensures tests will actually reflect the methods that will eventually be implemented.

#### *2.1.2.5. Layer Scoped Sub Tasking*

Esposito et al. (2025) found that AI‑generated code can easily breach architectural boundaries when given unrestricted access to a project. In CQRS and Clean Architecture, preserving layer separation ensures maintainability and reduces coupling risk. By scoping AI CLI context only to files within a designated layer, and explicitly constraining permitted dependencies, produced code will only interact with that layer. This should mitigate any breach of boundaries upholding architectural compliance.

This practice will be tested on the Archive Playlist feature, a complex feature involving high levels of business logic and database access. The implementation touches all three layers of the application. By applying strict layer scoped prompting during development, we can evaluate whether AI‑generated artefacts remain compliant with the architectural rules.

Figure 10 shows how each instance of the AI CLI tool has its workspace set to the layer relevant to it.

![][image7]

*Figure 10\. Parallel CLIs with Layer Scoped Workspaces*

### 2.1.3. Implementation Workflow {#2.1.3.-implementation-workflow}

Development will be completed with 3 implementations per feature:

* Control A — Feature implemented without AI CLI assistance, using standard procedures and the pre‑defined architecture.  
* Control B — Feature implemented with AI CLI usage but without any standard practices being employed.  
* Experimental — Feature implemented with AI CLI usage, applying only the assigned practice.

Each implementation will be completed in its entirety for the full feature set making up the MVP before moving onto the next. Each feature being completed will be forked from the control A branch, effectively resetting back to a known stable state. This configuration ensures validity by isolating the practice under review as the sole independent variable between runs, so any observed performance or compliance differences can be attributed to that practice rather than external factors. This is demonstrated in Figure 11\.

![][image8] 

*Figure 11\. Feature Branch Forking*

## 2.2. Results & Analysis {#2.2.-results-&-analysis}

### 2.2.1. Analysis Overview {#2.2.1.-analysis-overview}

Each practice is evaluated through direct comparison with two baseline implementations of the same feature: Control A and Control B

For every trial, this makes a total of three implementations, Control A, Control B, and the Experimental implementation trialling the practice. Metrics for each are recorded in accordance with section 1.3.3.

The analysis comparatively evaluates the experimental implementation against the control implementations, considering the magnitude and direction of change across each metric. Positive shifts (such as reduced development time or higher compliance scores) are taken as improvements resulting from the practice whilst negative shifts indicate degradation, and negligible change suggests limited measurable effect which could be due to the practice or the test scenario. This means an overall implementation may still be classified as a failure under the pass/fail criteria whilst the practice itself shows clear advantages. This ensures that promising methods are not disregarded due to a single failed run were improving the practice or selecting a better application scenario could enhance the practices impact.

These quantitative metrics are completed by qualitative insights from reviewer comments and developer observations that feed into a TAM survey. This combined approach ensures evaluation reflects both measurable performance changes and the practical implementation of the practice within Zircon’s workflow.

### 2.2.2. Results By Practice {#2.2.2.-results-by-practice}

#### *2.2.2.1. Persistent Context File*

This practice involved establishing a persistent, single‑setup context file (GEMINI.md) containing complete solution context, injected at the start of every AI CLI prompt. Tested on the Spotify Authentication Flow feature, the intent was to reduce time lost to repeated context provision, improving speed of delivery and consistency of responses across multi‑turn interactions.

| Practice ID | Practice | Completion Time | Error Count | Clean Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| SpotifyAuthenticationFlow-ControlA | N/A | 3 hours 16 minutes | 1 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| SpotifyAuthenticationFlow-ControlB | N/A | 1 hour 23 minutes | 1 | Fail (100) | Pass | Fail |
| SpotifyAuthenticationFlow-Experimental | Persistent Context File | 1 hour 7 minutes | 1 | Fail (100) | Pass | Fail |

*Figure 13\. Persistent Context File Results*

The resulting metrics show that completion time was reduced by 12% against Control B, with no change in error count and CQRS compliance maintained. However, Clean Architecture compliance was not improved due to a direct dependency on SpotifyAPI.Web within an abstraction assembly, leading to a failed overall.

TAM Perceived Usefulness scored 3.5, indicating moderate benefit. Perceived Ease of Use scored 4, reflecting straightforward adoption. PR review noted speed improvements and reduced time spent searching for context. However, the lack of mention of test assemblies in GEMINI.md led to recreation of the test assembly by the tool, demonstrating how this practice can be difficult to work with.

Overall, the practice achieved its objective of reducing delivery time but did not influence architectural compliance or error prevention. Benefits are maximised where context files are carefully curated to include all relevant artefacts to the solution.

#### *2.2.2.2. Prompt Scaffolding*

This practice decomposed the feature request into smaller, scoped prompts, each handled one at a time by the AI CLI. Tested on the Query Playlists feature, the aim was to produce more maintainable, well‑structured outputs, and align implementations with intended architecture.

| Practice ID | Practice | Completion Time | Error Count | Clean Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| QueryPlaylists-ControlA | N/A | 1 hour 55 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| QueryPlaylists-ControlB | N/A | 1 hour 5 minutes | 2 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| QueryPlaylists-Experimental | Prompt Scaffolding | 49 minutes | 1 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |

*Figure 14\. Prompt Scaffolding Results*

The resulting metrics show that prompt scaffolding achieved significant reductions in delivery time with a 23% drop against Control B, fewer errors than Control B, and full compliance with architectural rules giving an overall classification of pass.

TAM Perceived Usefulness 3.5, Perceived Ease of Use 5, this reflects typical developer decomposition processes. PR review noted improved clarity, ease of following AI reasoning, and scoped changes that simplified review. A nullable reference compilation error was encountered, consistent with common AI tooling behaviour.

Overall, prompt scaffolding improved delivery speed, maintained compliance, and provided tangible review advantages.

#### *2.2.2.3. Code Explanation and Variant Generation*

This practice directed the AI CLI to provide inline code commentary and generate implementation variants for complex logic. Tested on the Fetch Archived Playlists feature, the aim was to increase code transparency and provide alternative solutions for consideration during review.

| Practice ID | Practice | Completion Time | Error Count | Clean Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| FetchArchivedPlaylists-ControlA | N/A | 23 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| FetchArchivedPlaylists-ControlB | N/A | 19 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Fail | Fail |
| FetchArchivedPlaylists-Experimental | Code Explanation and Variant Generation | 18 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Fail | Fail |

*Figure 15\. Code Explanation and Variant Generation Results*

The resulting metrics show slight improvements in delivery time with 5% reduction against Control B, with error counts unchanged. Compliance matched Control B’s failure due to missed asymmetric layering opportunities, resulting in a failed classification.

TAM Perceived Usefulness 1.5 (low), Perceived Ease of Use 2.5. Comments were easy to produce but did not improve implementation quality. No variants were generated, as the tool assessed the feature as insufficiently complex. PR reviewers noted missed asymmetric layering opportunities.

Overall, the practice provided minimal measurable benefit for this test, with low perceived usefulness and no improvement in compliance.

#### *2.2.2.4. Assertion First Prompting*

This practice required the AI CLI to first produce abstractions and associated tests before implementing functionality, effectively applying Test‑Driven Development principles. Tested on the List Songs from Archive feature, the expectation was tighter compliance to architecture, early identification of design adjustments, and self‑evaluation by the tool.

| Practice ID | Practice | Completion Time | Error Count | Clean Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| ListSongsFromArchive-ControlA | N/A | 29 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| ListSongsFromArchive-ControlB | N/A | 20 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Fail | Fail |
| ListSongsFromArchive-Experimental | Assertion-First Prompting | 15 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |

*Figure 16\. Insertion First Prompting Results*

The resulting metrics show that this practice produced faster completion times with a 25% drop against Control B, maintained error-free compilation, and improved CQRS compliance over Control B. Overall classification was a Pass.

TAM Perceived Usefulness 5 (high), Perceived Ease of Use 4.5. PR notes highlighted the automatic self\-evaluation capability and correctness of asymmetric layering. The only difficulty noted in implementing this practice was ensuring all necessary abstractions existed to support the tests being created.

Overall, this practice was highly effective in improving compliance and preserving performance gains, with exceptionally strong perceived value.

#### *2.2.2.5. Layer Scoped Sub Tasking*

This practice initiated separate AI CLI instances scoped to individual architectural layers, with tasks broken down to fit to each layer. Tested on the Archive Playlist feature, it was expected to enforce strict layering, improve compliance, and reduce scope creep.

| Practice ID | Practice | Completion Time | Error Count | Clean Architecture Compliance | CQRS Compliance | Classification |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| ArchivePlaylist-ControlA | N/A | 2 hour 38 minutes | 1 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |
| ArchivePlaylist-ControlB | N/A | 1 hour 12 minutes | 4 | Fail (71) | Pass | Fail |
| ArchivePlaylist-Experimental | Layer Scoped Sub Tasking | 52 minutes | 0 | Pass (100) | Pass | Pass |

*Figure 17\. Layer Scoped Sub Tasking Results*

The resulting metrics show reduced delivery time with a 67% drop against Control A and 23% against Control B, elimination of all errors, and restored full compliance compared to Control B’s failure. Overall classification was a Pass.

TAM Perceived Usefulness 4.5, Perceived Ease of Use 3.0. Directory restructuring was necessary for effective scope enforcement of the CLI tool. Coordination challenges arose when multiple instances accessed the same abstraction, risking overwrites. However, tool efficiency was improved drastically thanks to being able to run the CLI tools in parallel, so long as they weren’t blocking each other. Additionally, additional context was easy to add to a CLI instance, such as the abstractions of other layers. 

Layer scoped sub tasking yielded strong architectural protection and error reduction, although required the solution to be in a compatible structure.

### 2.2.3. Experiment Patterns {#2.2.3.-experiment-patterns}

Across the practices trialled, some themes can be observed. Delivery times consistently improved over both controls, with the largest gains from Layer Scoped Sub Tasking and Persistent Context File, both of which narrowed or structured the tool’s working context. Comparing tool usage (seen in the results) one factor reducing implementation time was less file searching and context gathering by the tool, this is because it had fewer artefacts to scan to fulfil the prompt. Gains varied by practice, however, marginal improvements appeared where architectural relevance was limited, such as Code Explanation & Variant Generation.

Architectural compliance improved when restrictions were embedded directly into the workflow (Assertion First Prompting, Layer Scoped Sub Tasking) with measurable effects on maintaining Clean Architecture and CQRS. Practices focused only on interaction efficiency (Persistent Context File, Code Explanation) did not alter compliance and often reproduced the same violations found in Control B.

Error rates were the same or reduced, most notably where scope was clearly restricted (Layer Scoped Sub Tasking, Assertion First Prompting) reducing scope creep and runtime defects. Parallelised CLI workflows and generating abstractions pre-test were very effective at avoiding such issues. The opposite occurred without strict boundaries; larger context sometimes introduced scope creep as seen in Persistent Context File runs where unrelated artefacts were implemented.

Overall, strictly structuring how the tool interacts with context, even at the cost of restructuring the solution, produced the most consistent gains in accuracy, compliance, and efficiency, whilst purely informational enhancements carried higher variance and greater risk of unnecessary work.

### 2.2.4. Ethical Considerations in Data Handling {#2.2.4.-ethical-considerations-in-data-handling}

Even in an internal, non‑client trial, the use of AI tooling introduces data handling concerns. Proprietary code and solution data were included in prompts, requiring secure environments for running the CLI. Practices such as Persistent Context File concentrate high‑value information into a single artefact, increasing sensitivity and requiring review before external transmission to ensure that the environment doesn’t expose any data relating to other projects or sensitive data relating to Zircon Software Ltd.

# 3\. Impact {#3.-impact}

## 3.1. Critical Evaluation {#3.1.-critical-evaluation}

The trials confirmed the hypothesis that evaluating targeted AI‑CLI practices in controlled conditions identifies those delivering measurable gains in productivity and architectural compliance aligning with the SMART goals, forming a clear basis for their adoption at Zircon. 

All practices achieved reductions in completion time compared to the controls, with the greatest performance gains observed in methods that restricted or specified the model’s working scope. Layer Scoped Sub Tasking delivered 67% faster delivery than Control A 23% against Control B while fully maintaining Clean Architecture and CQRS compliance unlike Control B. This met the SMART objective of measurable improvement whilst also highlighting the operational value of enforcing structural boundaries at the solution level.

As a result of these findings, Zircon has now standardised solution directory structures across projects using a multi layered architecture. This was previously down to team preference, but now projects contain distinct layer directories containing assemblies with explicit abstraction boundaries, encapsulating the context of a layer from the perspective of the CLI tool. This separation enables straightforward application of Layer Scoped Sub Tasking, ensuring AI‑generated artefacts integrate predictably with existing workflows while preventing coupling between layers. This is a result of experimental outcomes driving business process refinement, turning what was once individualised project setup into a consistent organisation wide standard.

Other practices have been placed into a checklist that is run through before implementing a feature using the AI CLI. This checklist now forms part of the PDCA “plan” phase, getting developers to define acceptance criteria, break down the feature into small sequential tasks, aggregate relevant architectural context, and wherever possible, use the CLI to first generate runnable tests before writing implementation code. By creating this checklist, Zircon not only ensures that TDD is preserved in AI‑assisted work but sees the benefits of the other practices within this trial.

Methods improving the interaction with the CLI tools such as the Persistent Context File have had direct process impact. The context file created during experiments proved effective in sustaining context across multi‑turn sessions. It is now maintained from project startup, with defined content requirements covering architectural diagrams, key interfaces, coding conventions, solution layout, and any other project specific rules. As well as reducing individual feature delivery times, this artefact improves handover between teams and onboarding of new developers, acting as a source of architectural and implementation knowledge. This has reduced new developers’ time to contribute, which fits greatly with the responsive agile nature of Zircon.

In contrast, the Code Explanation and Variant Generation practice did not produce results that have had a meaningful impact on the organisation. The tool did not generate alternative implementations, as it assessed the scenario as insufficiently complex. While the current results show limited business value, it is possible that under further trials with more complex features that can be implemented in many ways, this practice could still deliver benefits.

The trials validate that AI CLI tooling, when used within defined boundaries, can be integrated into Zircon’s secure workflows without affecting compliance or data integrity. Practices that utilise explicit scope control or enforce verification loops contribute to both code quality and standardising repeatable workflows, an advantage when working in remote build environments or embedded systems projects where IDE‑integrated assistants are impractical. The use of directory structuring, checklist‑driven tool use, and context file maintenance at Zircon displays that these improvements are no longer experimental trials, and whilst there is room for further experimentation, these practices for now are an integral part of development at Zircon.

Additionally, the experimentation has shown measurable gains in productivity with their adoption triggering structured changes in project setup, the governance of AI tool usage, and internal knowledge management. These developments directly align with the SMART objectives, are relevant to Zircon’s quality and security standards, and integrate easily into existing processes. As a result, AI CLI practices have progressed from early experimentation to established practices that enhance delivery performance and help maintain Zircon’s competitive advantage.

## 3.2. Further Work {#3.2.-further-work}

While the practices trialled have provided a strong foundation for Zircon to adapt to their workflows, there are several key areas where further work could extend and validate these findings. This continuation would ensure that the practices identified here not only remain relevant but are adaptable to broader and more complex scenarios.

One area for further work is to perform model driven experimentation in development. In this context, model driven experimentation refers to situations where developers are operating without a well-defined implementation path or are working on the bleeding edge of a technology. These scenarios require rapid testing of multiple approaches to determine the one most fit for the job. Practices could be developed that use AI tooling to simulate, prototype, or branch alternative designs quickly, enabling developers to compare different architectural or implementation strategies before committing to a chosen path. This would be extremely beneficial when exploring unfamiliar frameworks, integration patterns, or optimising for untested performance conditions, providing structure to what can often be an open ended and uncertain process.

Another area is to explore additional means of using the tool that has not yet been trialled formally at Zircon. While this study focused on code generation and testing workflows, modern AI CLIs are capable of automated documentation generation, context aware commenting, and backlog refinement support. These capabilities could reduce the time a developer spends performing administrative tasks while improving codebase clarity, particularly in project with long life spans or multiple teams. Controlled trials would determine whether these uses deliver measurable productivity gains without compromising quality or compliance.

Whilst the methodologies used throughout these experiments have provided meaningful results for Zircon, improvements can still be made. Currently the recorded metrics provide a point of comparison that allows for an evaluative analysis, this provides the knowledge to understand whether the practice is beneficial. However, these metrics currently do not help understand why some practices are more effective than others, currently this is only done through speculative reasoning. Adding additional statistics could yield more granular insights. For example, recording the time spent by the tool “working”, the active processing time from prompt submission to a usable output, would allow better insight into why a feature was implemented faster under the use of a particular practice.

With greater experience in applying these practices, Zircon could also identify targeted refinements to those already shown to be valuable. For instance, Layer Scoped Sub Tasking could be enhanced by implementing a dedicated context file for each layer, preserving layer specific reasoning, reducing the amount of time the tool spends gathering context, and reducing cross layer noise. By adjusting practices iteratively workflows can evolve alongside project needs and tooling capabilities, ensuring that the most effective versions of these methods are captured and standardised.

To assess the long-term viability of practices, future trials should apply identified practices to a project from startup to delivery over an extended timeline, involving a complete development team rather than a single developer. This would allow insight into how these practices influence collaborative workflows, QA processes, and architecture maintainability throughout the full delivery lifecycle. It would also provide insight into whether efficiency improvements hold over time as feature scope expands, the backlog shifts, and architectural knowledge matures.

Implementing extended testing in the Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act (PDCA) framework would allow for continuous improvement of both the practices and supporting organisational standards. Model‑driven experimentation, expanded usage scenarios, and iterative refinements informed by team feedback would ensure evaluation remains relevant in the context of both software development and the AI tools themselves.

Overall, further work should push AI CLI usage from targeted productivity enhancement into a strategic enabler for Zircon’s development processes. By diversifying test scenarios, expanding metrics captured, and validating practices in long‑term team projects, Zircon can build a long-term integration framework tailored to the organisation that balances speed, compliance, and maintainability, helping to enable the organisation to adapt quickly to future innovations while maintaining competitive advantage.
